text: You're given an integer array called nums. You start at index zero. Each value, nums at i, is the maximum forward jump from index i. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index. You can assume the last index is always reachable.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — from index i, I can land anywhere from i plus one, up to i plus nums at i. Forward only. I return a count, not the path. And since the end is always reachable, I never need to return minus one. Is that right?
Yes. Just the count, and you can trust the guarantee.

Okay. One fact from Jump Game one helps a lot here. If I can reach index j, I can reach every index before j too, because the jump could just stop shorter. So, the cells I can reach is always a prefix, not a random set. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length is between one and ten to the fourth, and every value is between zero and one thousand.

Got it. n can be one — then I'm already on the last index, so the answer is zero. The biggest sum, i plus nums at i, is at most ten thousand nine hundred ninety-eight, so an int is fine. Let me run through the example. Two, three, one, one, four: one jump gets me to index one or two, and from index one a jump of three lands on index four. So the answer is two. The second example, two, three, zero, one, four, is also two by the same path — the zero at index two doesn't matter, because I never stand there.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be dynamic programming: D P at j is the fewest jumps to reach j, and each i relaxes every j it can reach. Correct, but order n times the max jump — about ten to the seventh here. I'd keep it as a checker, not the answer. This problem reminds me of B F S shortest path. Fewest jumps is fewest edges, and every edge costs one, so I can think in layers: layer k is the cells I first reach in exactly k jumps. And the prefix fact pays off — each layer is a contiguous range that starts right after the last one ends. So I don't need a queue; a layer is just a right edge. My job is to find where each layer ends while scanning left to right.

Here's the plan. It's B F S, but with two numbers instead of a queue: cur-end, the right edge of the current layer, and next-end, the farthest one more jump can reach. First, scan i from zero to n minus two. Second, at each cell, raise next-end to i plus nums at i. Third, when i reaches cur-end, the layer is done — add one jump and move cur-end to next-end. The key idea: the code never picks which cell to jump from — it only tracks how far each layer goes. One thing worth flagging — the loop stops at n minus two. Scanning the last index fires the check one extra time, so the answer is always one too high. A queue-based B F S works too, but this is constant space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Three ints at zero — step, cur-end, next-end — and one loop while i is less than the size minus one. Inside, next-end takes the max with i plus nums at i; then, if cur-end equals i, step goes up and cur-end becomes next-end. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the order inside the loop matters. Next-end must update before the check, because cell i belongs to the layer I'm closing. Swap them and the first layer closes with edge zero, so example one returns one instead of two. Also, size minus one is unsigned, so there's one harmless sign-compare warning; storing n as an int first removes it.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one: two, three, one, one, four, expected two. The row that matters is i equals two: it's cur-end, so layer one closes — step becomes two, and cur-end moves to four, which covers the last index. Return two. Now the case that shows why I never pick a cell: four, one, one, three, one, one, one, answer two. The best path is zero, three, six, through the middle of layer one. Always jumping as far as possible takes three jumps, which is wrong. Corner cases: a single zero gives zero, four ones gives three, and ten thousand ones gives nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine, the worst case.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear — one pass up to n minus two, with no early exit. The space complexity is constant, three integers. The largest next-end is ten thousand nine hundred ninety-eight, so an int is safe. I'd test this against a B F S checker: two hundred sixty-one thousand six hundred cases, zero mismatches. The trap worth knowing: counting a jump every time next-end improves passes both official examples, but fails two, two, zero — it says two, and the right answer is one. Oh, one more thing — this code trusts the guarantee and never returns minus one. Three, two, one, zero, four returns two, even though index four can't be reached. If the guarantee could break, I'd return minus one when a layer closes with next-end still stuck at i.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed it as a B F S by layers, and used the prefix fact to show each layer is a range, so cur-end and next-end replace the queue. You showed with four, one, one, three, one, one, one why the code must not pick a jump: the best jump comes from the middle of a layer, and jump-farthest takes three. And you nailed the two order details — stopping at n minus two, and updating before the check — plus the trap that passes both examples but fails two, two, zero. Good work.
